guideTitle: Best Sliding Compound Miter Saws Under $500 (2026)
metaDescription: Five sliding compound miter saws at or under $500, from a cordless 12 inch DEWALT to 10 inch corded models, compared on crosscut width, bevel and rail design.
expertTake: The DEWALT DCS785B is the pick for most pros because a 12 inch double bevel sliding head cuts 14 inches wide and 6-1/2 inch baseboard standing up, with no cord to trip over. The SKIL MS6305 is the value pick for a home shop that wants dual bevel and a shadow line at the lowest tier here. Skip a sliding saw entirely if you only trim baseboard, because a fixed 10 inch saw holds its angles better and costs less than any saw in this guide. The extra budget over an entry slider mostly buys rail stiffness, bevel flexibility and, for the DEWALT, freedom from the cord.
introParagraphs: A sliding compound miter saw adds rails or arms that carry the blade forward and back, so a small blade can cut a board far wider than its radius. The extra reach is the whole point, but it comes with moving parts that must stay tight for the saw to cut square.

This guide explains what the upper end of a larger budget buys in a sliding saw, how rail design and bevel type change accuracy, and which spec sheet claims need a skeptical read. The picks are listed above, with the reviews below. Listing prices move, and the cap reflects prices when this guide was updated.

products.name: DEWALT DCS785B 20V MAX XR 12 Inch Double Bevel Sliding Miter Saw (Tool Only)
products.description:
Regenerative braking captures the blade's spin energy when you release the trigger and sends part of it back to the battery, which stretches runtime on a saw that starts and stops hundreds of times a day. A 12 inch blade on a sliding head crosscuts up to 14 inches horizontally, and it can cut 6-1/2 inch baseboard standing up against the fence. It is also the first 12 inch DEWALT miter saw compatible with the full range of 20V MAX and FLEXVOLT batteries.

The tradeoff is that the listing is bare tool, with no battery or charger, so the real cost depends on what you own. Compared with the corded saws in this guide, the DCS785B gives up nothing in capacity but adds weight when a large pack is on board. Versus the SKIL MS6305, it cuts a larger board with a larger blade and cuts the cord. For a trim crew that moves between rooms, it saves hours of extension-cord shuffling.

Ownership: keep a spare pack charged, since a 12 inch blade drains a pack on long cutting days. Check the fence square and the rails for play before critical cuts, and clean the rails of dust. Use a good 80-tooth blade for finish trim, and store batteries out of heat.
products.bestFor: Trim crews who own 20V MAX or FLEXVOLT batteries and want a 12 inch cordless slider.
pros: 14 inch horizontal crosscut handles wide boards
Regenerative braking returns energy to the battery
Double bevel avoids flipping boards
Cordless design removes extension-cord hassle
cons: Tool only, so batteries and a charger cost extra
Heavy with a large battery installed
Highest relative price in the roundup

products.name: Evolution R185SMS+ 210mm Sliding Miter Saw, Cuts Wood and Metal
products.description:
A multi-material blade and a high-torque gearbox let this saw cut steel, aluminum and wood without changing machines. Dry metal cutting produces less heat and fewer sparks than an abrasive chop saw, and the cut edge needs little cleanup. The 15 amp motor reduces load through gearing, and the sliding head extends crosscut width beyond the 210 millimeter blade's radius.

The tradeoff is scale. An 8-1/4 inch blade cuts less deep and less wide than a 10 or 12 inch saw, so it is not a trim saw for tall crown. Against the DEWALT DCS785B, this machine cuts metal that the DEWALT cannot, but finish cuts in wood are rougher. For a shop that cuts conduit, angle iron and framing, the versatility is the reason to buy.

Ownership: wear eye and ear protection, since metal cutting is loud. Metal chips collect around the base and rails, so clean them out after each session. Use the right blade for the material, and replace it when teeth dull. The sliding rails need light lubrication to stay smooth.
products.bestFor: Fabricators and remodelers who cut conduit, angle iron and wood on one saw.
pros: Multi-material blade cuts steel, aluminum and wood
Dry cutting leaves a clean edge with fewer sparks
15 amp high-torque gearbox handles metal
Sliding head extends crosscut width
cons: 8-1/4 inch blade limits depth and width
Wood finish quality trails dedicated trim saws
Metal cutting is loud and throws chips

products.name: SKIL MS6305-00 10 Inch Dual Bevel Sliding Compound Miter Saw, 15 Amp
products.description:
A dual bevel head tilts both left and right with positive stops at 48 degrees and 45 degrees left, 0 degrees and 45 degrees right, which spares you from flipping a long board to cut an opposite angle. A 15 amp motor at 4,800 RPM drives the 10 inch blade through hardwood trim. An LED shadow line projects the blade's edge onto the wood, which shows the true kerf better than a laser dot.

Compared with the DEWALT DCS785B, the SKIL is smaller, corded and far lower in relative price, but it crosscuts less width. Compared with the KSEIBI and Marvtool, it offers a dual bevel where those are single bevel. For a home shop that builds shelving and trim, the SKIL is the best balance of features and cost.

Ownership: check the fence for square and adjust the bevel stops with a square before the first cut. Slide rails need dust cleaned from them, and the bearings may need tightening if the head wobbles. Use a better blade than the stock one for finish work, and clean the LED lens so the shadow line stays crisp.
products.bestFor: Home shops that want a dual bevel sliding saw at the lowest relative price.

Lowest relative price in the roundup
cons: Narrower crosscut than the 12 inch DEWALT

products.name: KSEIBI 10 Inch Sliding Compound Miter Saw, 15 Amp Dual Rail
products.description:
Twin linear slide rails carry the blade forward and back, and a dual-rail design resists twist better than a single arm. A 15 amp motor delivering about 1,800 watts gives strong corded power, and a 255 millimeter blade is the 10 inch standard. The miter table swings 45 degrees both ways while the head bevels in one direction.

The tradeoff is bevel and brand support. A single bevel means flipping boards for opposite cuts, which the SKIL MS6305 avoids. The brand is less established than DEWALT, so parts and service are thinner. Compared with the Marvtool, the KSEIBI's dual rails are a more robust slide, and the listing emphasizes strong consistent power. For a shop that crosscuts wide boards at a low tier, it is a sensible choice.

Ownership: check the rails for smoothness and the base for flatness on arrival. Keep the rails clean and lightly oiled, and tighten the fence bolts. A better blade than the stock one improves finish, and a stand or bench with clamps keeps the saw stable.
products.bestFor: Shops that crosscut wide boards and want dual rails on a corded 10 inch saw.

products.name: Marvtool 10 Inch Sliding Compound Miter Saw, 15 Amp, 5,000 RPM
products.description:
A 36-tooth blade is a rough-cut blade, suited to framing and rough trim, and the saw spins it at 5,000 RPM, the fastest speed in this roundup. A transparent blade guard helps you see the cut line, and an extension table supports long boards. The listing describes left miter angles from 0 to 45 degrees and an adjustable base.

The tradeoff is finish. A 36-tooth blade tears the face of trim and plywood, so replace it with an 80-tooth blade for any finish work. Compared with the SKIL MS6305 it has a single bevel and fewer features, and compared with the KSEIBI it has a less robust slide. It is the lowest tier of the sliding saws, aimed at the garage woodworker.

Ownership: expect to spend time on setup, squaring the fence and checking the rails. Keep rails clean, and use the extension table for long boards. A better blade is the first upgrade, and clamping the saw to a bench makes it safer.
products.bestFor: Garage woodworkers who want a sliding saw for framing and shelving at the lowest tier.
pros: 5,000 RPM is the fastest no-load speed in the roundup
Extension table supports long boards
Transparent blade guard improves sight lines
15 amp motor with a sliding head at a low tier

buyingCriteria.explanation: Crosscut width is the widest board the saw can cut in one pass. The DEWALT DCS785B cuts up to 14 inches, while 10 inch sliders cut about 12. Capacity at 45 degrees drops by roughly a third. Many buyers forget that wide capacity is quoted at 0 degrees. Measure your widest board against the stated capacity with a margin of an inch, because the number assumes a flat board held tight against the fence.

Rails carry the blade, and any play makes cuts wander. The KSEIBI uses twin linear rails, which resist twist. Check for wobble in the head at full extension. A sloppy rail ruins accuracy on wide cuts. To check a rail, extend the head fully, push sideways on the handle and watch the blade; more than a hair of movement means the saw will cut wide boards out of square.

A single bevel tilts one direction, so opposite angles require flipping the board. A double bevel tilts both ways. The DEWALT DCS785B and SKIL MS6305 are dual. Flipping long boards wastes time and risks errors. The cost of flipping boards adds up on a house of crown and base, which is why trim contractors usually pay for dual bevel.

A 12 inch blade cuts deeper and wider than 10 inch, and tooth count sets finish. A 36-tooth blade like the Marvtool's is rough, and 80 teeth cut trim cleanly. A saw is only as good as its blade. A cheap saw with a good 80-tooth blade often cuts better than an expensive saw with a rough blade, so budget for the blade first.

A cordless slider like the DCS785B avoids extension cords but needs large packs. Corded saws run forever. Choose cordless if you own the platform and move between jobs. A cordless slider is also quieter at idle, which matters in occupied homes.

A tall fence supports base molding standing vertically. The DCS785B supports 6-1/2 inch baseboard. A short fence makes tall trim lean and cut crooked. For base molding taller than the fence, add a sacrificial auxiliary fence of plywood rather than letting the trim lean.

specDecoder.meaning: This is the maximum board width the saw cuts in one pass. It depends on blade size and slide length.
specDecoder.watchFor: The DEWALT's 14 inches is at 0 degrees, and it shrinks at bevels. Always measure crosscut capacity yourself on the first board.

specDecoder.meaning: This captures energy when the blade slows and returns it to the battery. It extends runtime.
specDecoder.watchFor: The gain depends on how often you stop the blade. Do not expect the same gain when you cut at full speed all day.

specDecoder.meaning: Twin rails carry the head, resisting twist. A single arm is lighter but flexes more.
specDecoder.watchFor: The KSEIBI lists dual rails, but quality of bearings matters. Rails need regular cleaning regardless of the brand.

specDecoder.meaning: Tooth count sets finish: fewer teeth cut fast and rough, more teeth cut slow and smooth.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Marvtool's 36-tooth blade is for rough work. A fine blade on a rough saw still gives rough results.

specDecoder.meaning: Bevel stops are positive detents at common angles. They speed setup.
specDecoder.watchFor: The SKIL lists four, and other listings do not state their count. Count the stops before you buy, because they save minutes on every project.

howWeEvaluated.title: Crosscut capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated capacity, from the DEWALT's 14 inches to the 10 inch sliders. Capacity decides which boards fit. We cross-checked each claim against blade radius and slide length to see if it was plausible.

howWeEvaluated.title: Slide quality
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at rail design, favoring dual rails. Twin rails earned credit, but we noted that bearing quality matters as much as rail count.

howWeEvaluated.title: Bevel flexibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We separated single and dual bevel saws, since flipping boards wastes time. Dual bevel saved more time in our analysis than any other feature for long trim runs.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power and platform
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared corded 15 amp motors and the cordless DCS785B. We counted battery requirements for the cordless saw as part of its cost.

howWeEvaluated.title: Relative value
howWeEvaluated.description: We used price tier to compare what extra spending buys. We compared tiers rather than amounts, and flagged where an extra tier adds only a convenience.

maintenance.why: A fence off square ruins miters. Use a square against the blade. Use a brush rather than compressed air if dust packs into the bearings.
Dust stiffens rails and hurts accuracy. Light oil keeps them smooth. A drop of light machine oil is enough.
A dull blade strains the motor. Fresh blades cut cleaner. Choose a blade with the right tooth count for the work.
Rail play makes cuts wander. Tighten bearings if needed. Mark the bearing adjustment before changing it.
Clogged ports reduce collection. Clear them with a rod. Check the dust hose for kinks.

faq.q: Do I need a sliding saw?
faq.a: If you cut boards wider than 6 inches, yes. For trim only, a fixed saw is stiffer. Choose by board width. A fixed saw plus a circular saw for wide boards is a common alternative.
It buys a 10 inch corded slider or a cordless 12 inch bare tool. Listing prices move, so check the live cost. Prices vary between sellers, so compare tiers rather than a single listing.

faq.q: How long do sliding saws last?
faq.a: With care, many years. Rails and bearings wear first. Lubricate the rails and keep the saw covered in a dusty shop.
For long trim runs, yes. It saves flipping boards. It also reduces tear-out on the far side of the cut.
Only with a saw and blade made for it, like the Evolution. Wood blades are not safe for metal. Wear eye and hearing protection regardless.
A stable bench helps. Clamp the saw down. Without a stand, a sheet of plywood clamped to sawhorses works.
